Name: recite_vs_execute
Title: It Can State the Rule but Runs a Different One: The Recitation-Execution Gap in LLM Procedural Knowledge
Short Hypothesis: An LLM carries a procedure's declarative description (the rule it can recite) and the executable pathway that runs in the forward pass as partially distinct, only weakly causally coupled representations. This predicts one specific double dissociation — the recitation-execution gap: a model recites a rule correctly yet executes a contradicting heuristic. We make three graded, falsifiable claims. (H1) The gap is a distinct, gradable failure mode whose rate exceeds a shared-competence null and rises with procedure complexity. (H2) The recited-rule representation is present but only weakly causally coupled to the execution circuit, so patching it from a correct run into a gap case only partially restores rule-consistent execution. (H3) Steering the execution circuit toward the recited-rule direction makes the model follow its own stated rule — altering intermediate computation, not merely nudging output logits — without changing what it recites. We claim novelty in the specific double-dissociation behavior and its causal coupling/repair test, not a new general theory of procedural knowledge.
Related Work: Prior work shows arithmetic is a 'bag of heuristics' rather than an algorithm (Arithmetic Without Algorithms, 2024) and undergoes 'algorithmic phase transitions' across subtasks (2024); procedural pretraining installs modular reusable circuits, mostly in attention (Procedural Pretraining, 2026; Modular Structures, 2025); Programming by Backprop (2025) finds execution-from-instruction is far less reliable than in-context instructions; procedures generalize poorly across code/graph/NL representations (Generalize Procedures Across Representations, 2026); circuit-reuse work (2023) shows shared algorithmic building blocks. Novelty here is in SETTING and BEHAVIOR plus a causal MECHANISM test, not a new theory. Explicit deltas: (1) all prior work characterizes the enacted procedure or its reusability, but measures execution alone; we instrument recitation and execution on the SAME item and isolate their dissociation as the target phenomenon. Closest are emerging 2026 dissociation papers on declarative-vs-procedural knowledge; the concrete delta is that they compare separate probes or separate prompts, whereas we (a) require, per item, a verified-correct recited rule and a well-defined contradicting heuristic output, giving a per-item gap label they cannot produce; (b) run activation patching of the recited-rule representation into a failing execution run to test causal coupling directly, rather than inferring dissociation from probe separability; and (c) test repair — binding recitation into execution — with a specificity control that recitation itself is unchanged. This is not a rewording: our claim is a causal-coupling statement about two representations in one forward pass, testable by patching/steering, whereas the dissociation literature makes correlational representational claims. This also differs from my prior say-vs-use proposal, which concerns implicit *use of a fact* rather than *execution of a procedure that contradicts a correctly-stated rule*.
Abstract: Large language models can often correctly state how to perform a procedure — the rule for pluralization, a sorting comparator, a modular-arithmetic step, a game rule — yet, when they carry it out, they execute a different, usually simpler procedure that contradicts the rule they just recited. We call this the recitation-execution gap. We make the phenomenon concrete with two operational objects rather than a metaphor: the 'recited-rule representation' is a linearly decodable residual-stream direction, extracted during the recitation forward pass, that encodes which rule the model stated; the 'execution circuit' is the set of attention/MLP components whose activation patching flips the enacted output between the rule-consistent and heuristic branches. Our hypothesis is that these two are partially distinct and only weakly causally coupled. We separate three claims and the evidence for each. Behavioral (H1): across procedure families (string/morphology rules, list operations, modular and base-conversion arithmetic, rule-following games) we elicit and verify the model's stated rule and separately measure whether execution obeys it, testing that the gap rate exceeds a pre-specified shared-competence null and grows with complexity. Representational: linear probes show the recited-rule direction carries information beyond the enacted execution state (probes establish separability, not mechanism). Causal (H2/H3): activation patching tests whether the recited-rule representation is present-but-uncoupled during execution, and a steering intervention tests whether injecting it into the execution circuit binds recitation to execution — making the model follow its own stated rule while leaving recitation and unrelated procedures intact, with an ablation confirming the fix changes intermediate computation rather than only output logits. So what: if the gap is real, a model's recited rationale is not evidence that it will execute that rule, which directly affects tool invocation, agentic workflows, self-explanation faithfulness, and instruction-following audits — a recited procedure should be treated as an unverified claim, and steering offers a lightweight way to enforce stated rules. The hypothesis is falsifiable: it is refuted if recitation and execution reflect one shared competence (no residual interaction), if the recited-rule direction is not separable from the execution state, or if patching/steering fails to shift execution. Experiments span GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, evaluating gap prevalence, probe separability, causal coupling, execution recovery, and specificity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H0 — procedure dataset construction, incl. one clean primary family): Build controlled items where a rule can be both stated and executed and where a contradicting heuristic output is well-defined, so the gap is measurable. Data: constructed programmatically across four families — (a) string/morphology transforms (reverse, remove-vowels, regular vs irregular inflection), (b) list operations (sort-by-key, filter, dedup), (c) explicit-algorithm arithmetic (modular addition, base conversion, carrying), (d) stated-move rule games — 400 items per family, 1,600 total, each with a canonical rule-consistent output and a plausible heuristic-consistent output. We designate family (c) modular/base-conversion arithmetic as the CLEAN PRIMARY family (unambiguous rule, single decision point, machine-checkable heuristic) on which the core mechanistic claims (Exp 4-6) are established first; other families provide breadth (Exp 7). Operational criteria per family are fixed in advance: 'rule-consistent output' = the output of the canonical procedure; 'heuristic-consistent output' = the output of the named contradicting shortcut (e.g. ignore-carry, apply-regular-inflection, sort-by-surface-token). Model: Llama-3-8B, frozen; greedy decoding, temperature 0, 3 prompt seeds. Decisive metric (first): fraction of items for which rule-consistent and heuristic-consistent outputs are distinct AND a matched-difficulty control confirms the heuristic is a real attractor (a model prompted only with examples produces the heuristic output > 50% of the time). Convincing: >= 1,200 items pass, >= 250 per family. Indecision band: 800-1,200 pass — reduced per-family power, reported; below 800 the heuristic is not a genuine competitor and the gap is ill-defined. Negative (heuristic never competes) means there is no shortcut to contradict recitation and the phenomenon cannot be studied on these families.

Experiment 2 (H0 — recitation elicitation and verification, with prompt/format controls): Establish, per item, that the model can state the correct rule, so execution failures are not mere ignorance, and that the label is not a prompt or answer-format artifact. Data: passing items from Experiment 1. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; elicit the stated rule in natural language/pseudocode. Operational criterion for 'recites the correct rule': the stated rule, when executed by a reference interpreter on 5 held-out probe inputs, reproduces the canonical outputs on all 5 (behavioral verification, not string match to a template). Controls: 3 recitation prompt paraphrases and 2 answer formats (free-form vs constrained); an item counts as reliably reciting only if it passes under >= 2/3 paraphrases, quantifying prompt sensitivity. Systems compared: reference-interpreter check plus an LLM judge (GPT-4o) with human spot-checks on a 100-item calibration sample. Decisive metric (first): fraction of items whose recited rule is verified correct across paraphrases (the 'analysis set'); report judge-vs-human agreement (Cohen's kappa). Convincing: analysis set >= 800 items with judge-human kappa >= 0.8 and paraphrase-stable labels. Indecision band: kappa 0.6-0.8 — judge noisy; fall back to interpreter-check-only labels and report shrinkage. Negative (analysis set < 400 or kappa < 0.6) means recitation cannot be reliably verified and downstream gap claims are unfounded.

Experiment 3 (H1, behavioral — recitation-execution gap is a distinct, gradable failure mode): Test that models recite a correct rule yet execute the contradicting heuristic, at a rate exceeding a pre-specified shared-competence null. Data: analysis set. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; classify each item as (a) recite-execute gap, (b) both correct, (c) both wrong. Pre-registered null: recitation and execution are two Bernoulli readouts of one latent per-item competence theta with independent noise; parameters fit on the both-correct and both-wrong cells only, then used to predict the off-diagonal gap mass (logistic model; permutation test, 1,000 permutations). This specifies the gap statistic before seeing the off-diagonal. Gap rate is regressed on rule length/step count and input difficulty. Decisive metric (first): residual recite-execute interaction (log-odds, CI) beyond the null, and gap prevalence per family. Convincing: interaction CI excludes 0 and gap cell >= 10% in >= 3 of 4 families, rising with complexity. Indecision band: gap cell 4-10% or interaction CI just excluding 0 in <3 families — weak/partial gap. Negative (interaction CI includes 0) means recitation and execution reflect one competence, refuting H1.

Experiment 4 (H1, representational — separable recited-rule and execution-state representations; probes establish separability, not mechanism): Test that the recited rule carries information distinct from the enacted execution state during the forward pass. Data: analysis set (primary family first) with per-item gap labels. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; train a rule-representation probe (decode recited-rule identity, trained on the recitation forward pass) and an execution-state probe (decode which branch/heuristic is being applied) via logistic regression at each layer (seeds {0,1,2}, 5-fold, label-shuffle null). Decisive metric (first): residualized unique AUROC of the recited-rule direction during the EXECUTION pass, after partialling out the execution-state signal. Convincing: unique rule AUROC >= 0.65 and execution-state probe >= 0.75 at its best layer. Indecision band: unique rule AUROC 0.55-0.65 — mostly shared representation. Negative (<= 0.55, at shuffle) means recited rule and execution share one representation, weakening H1's 'distinct representations'. Note (scoping): a positive probe result is necessary but NOT sufficient for the mechanism claim; Exp 5-6 carry the causal burden.

Experiment 5 (H2, causal — recited rule is weakly causally coupled to execution): Test the coupling strength causally. Data: gap items and matched both-correct runs of the same procedure (primary family first). Model: Llama-3-8B frozen; patch the recited-rule representation from a both-correct run into a failing execution run at the identified layers/positions; reverse control ablates the recited-rule representation in both-correct runs; also patch execution-circuit components to confirm they carry the enacted procedure. Systems compared: rule-patch vs execution-component-patch vs random-position patch. Decisive metric (first): execution-flip rate = fraction of gap items whose output becomes rule-consistent under the rule-patch, minus random-patch rate. The experiment reports which of three regimes holds: present-but-uncoupled (< 10 points), weak-but-usable coupling (10-40 points), or strong coupling (> 40 points). Convincing (supports H2's 'weak but usable coupling'): flip rate 10-40 points. Indecision band: 8-12 points straddles the uncoupled/weak boundary; report as boundary and defer to Experiment 6. Negative direction for the intervention program: if flip rate < 8 points, H3's steering is unlikely to work and we say so up front.

Experiment 6 (H3, causal — binding the recited rule into execution fixes behavior without changing recitation, and changes intermediate computation not just logits): Test the steering claim. Data: analysis set, item-disjoint train/test (primary family first, then breadth via Exp 7); steering vector = mean residual difference (rule-consistent-execution minus heuristic-execution matched states), seeds {0,1,2}, rank <= 4. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen except the injected direction. Systems compared: rule-binding steering, execution-state-direction amplification, fine-tuning on rule-consistent examples, random-direction control, and a logit-nudge control (directly boosting the target answer token). Decisive metric (first): execution-recovery rate (gap items now rule-consistent) net of random. Mechanism ablation (required): (i) recovery must exceed the logit-nudge control, and (ii) under steering, the execution-state probe (Exp 4) at intermediate layers must flip from heuristic to rule-consistent BEFORE the final token — showing changed intermediate computation, not only output logits. Secondary specificity: recited rule unchanged (recitation accuracy delta), both-correct items still correct, accuracy on unrelated procedures, fluency (perplexity delta). Convincing: net recovery >= 25% with recitation and both-correct accuracy dropping < 3 points, beating both execution-amplification and logit-nudge, with intermediate-probe flip confirmed. Indecision band: recovery 12-25% or both-correct drop 3-6 points — partial fix; report. Negative (no better than logit-nudge/random, or recitation changes, or no intermediate-probe flip) refutes H3.

Experiment 7 (H1/H3 — transfer and architecture generality): Test that the gap and its fix generalize across items/families and models. Data: items partitioned by family; steering vector trained on the primary family, applied to held-out families. Models: GPT-J-6B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, frozen; re-run Experiments 3-6, seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric (first): cross-family execution-recovery relative to within-family, plus replication of the gap prevalence (Experiment 3) per model. Convincing: cross-family recovery >= 40% of within-family AND gap replicates in >= 2 of 3 models. Indecision band: replication in 1 model or cross-family 25-40% — model/procedure-specific. Negative (no transfer/replication) confines findings to one model. Report whether larger models show a smaller gap.

Experiment 8 (H1 — source of the gap; auxiliary): Quantify how much the gap is execution defaulting to a well-primed heuristic. Data: analysis set. Model: Llama-3-8B frozen (plus Pythia 1.4B/2.8B/6.9B for scale). Decisive metric (first): partial regression coefficients of gap prevalence on (procedure complexity, heuristic-shortcut availability = how strongly the contradicting procedure fits the surface pattern, input-distribution familiarity), with CIs. Convincing: heuristic-availability coefficient CI-excludes 0 and dominates the others, gap decreasing across Pythia scale. Indecision band: coefficient CI half-width overlapping 0 by < 0.02 — sources entangled; report inconclusive. Negative (heuristic-availability not significant) means the gap has another driver, qualifying the mechanistic claim. This experiment is auxiliary: it explains but does not gate the core H1-H3 claims.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The gap could reflect that the model does not truly 'know' the rule despite reciting it (recitation as surface pattern, not internalized procedure); the reference-interpreter verification (Exp 2, requiring the stated rule to reproduce outputs on held-out probes) and the causal patching test (Exp 5) mitigate this, and a graded result remains informative.

Recitation and execution representations may be entangled rather than separable; probe separability (Exp 4) is explicitly treated as necessary-not-sufficient, and the steering/patching tests (Exp 5-6), not probe onset, are decisive; partial dissociation would weaken the strong claim while still being informative.

Defining a single 'execution-state' representation is hard when procedures are multi-step and distributed; the clean primary family (modular/base arithmetic) has a localizable single decision point, and primary analysis restricts to procedures with a localizable branch/decision point and reports coverage.

Steering could merely nudge output logits toward the target answer rather than change computation; Exp 6 adds an explicit logit-nudge control and requires an intermediate-layer probe flip before the final token, so a pure-logit fix is detected and does not count as support.

The binding intervention could break correctly-executed procedures or degrade fluency if the injected direction overlaps useful features; the both-correct and unrelated-procedure specificity controls are central and utility may be capped.
A single transferable binding vector may not exist if coupling is procedure-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Recitation labels could be prompt- or format-sensitive; Exp 2 requires paraphrase-stable labels across 3 prompts and 2 formats, but residual prompt sensitivity may shrink the analysis set.
Findings on 6-8B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget; Exp 7 reports the gap-vs-scale trend as partial evidence.
